quote: The Gram-Schmidt procedure turns any set of independent vectors into an orthonormal basis by subtracting projections one at a time.
problem: The chapter uses a `didyouknow` environment three times (sections on bases, determinants and Paper connection). It is not among the environments the bible defines, so it may not compile. The boxes are historical asides the bible's voice rule excludes ("no filler, no motivational asides"), they carry unsourced dates, and Gram-Schmidt is never taught in the chapter. One box sits at the top of the mandatory Paper connection section. "Gram-Schmidt" also uses a hyphen where paired names take an en dash.
fix: Delete the three didyouknow boxes (including the DYK-BEGIN/END comments). If the Gram--Schmidt remark is wanted, put one plain sentence after the projection subsection, with an en dash.

quote: subtracting the fixed vector $\Delta$ from the targets is the same as adding it to the prediction
problem: The sign is reversed relative to the paper's Eq. (3). There the targets are t̃_n = t_n + Δ_n (Δ is added), and the identity t̃_n − E_n = t_n − (E_n − Δ_n) says this equals subtracting Δ from the prediction.
fix: Replace with: "adding the fixed vector $\Delta$ to the targets ($\tilde t=t+\Delta$) is the same as subtracting it from the prediction and scoring against the raw zeros".

quote: This is the linear-algebra core of several statements in the paper.
problem: The counting argument (more columns than rows gives an exact fit) is contradicted by the paper's own Table I. Fits with M larger than the number of training zeros still leave sizeable in-sample error: 300 zeros/M=400 gives 0.120, 400/M=600 gives 0.064, 800/M=900 gives 0.103. Exact fit of 500 zeros needs M≈900, not M>500. So the linearized matrix is far from full row rank in practice (the paper's coverage law Mπ/L > 2√E). The chapter never says this, and a student will be misled.
fix: Add after this paragraph: "Shape alone does not guarantee full row rank. In Table I the fits with more coefficients than levels (300/400, 400/600, 800/900) still have in-sample rms 0.120, 0.064 and 0.103, and 500 zeros are reproduced exactly only near M=900. The sensitivity matrix is effectively rank deficient until the cosines resolve the wavefunctions (the coverage law, Chapter~\ref{ch:fitting})."

quote: is what one expects when a nearly full-rank model has more coefficients than training levels
problem: Answer 19 presents near-zero in-sample error as the expected result of M exceeding the number of levels. Parts (a) and (c) of the same problem have M above the number of levels, yet Table I gives in-sample rms 0.120 and 0.103 for them. The answer hides that contradiction.
fix: Add to the answer: "Note that (a) and (c) are also underdetermined by shape, yet Table I reports in-sample rms 0.120 and 0.103. Their matrices are not effectively of full row rank, so counting columns gives only an upper bound on what can be fitted."

quote: explains why the paper can say both
problem: The beat-the-null inequality is exact only for the uncentered cosine, whereas the paper reports Pearson correlation. With "cos θ ≲ 0" the conclusion is not exact: a slightly positive cosine allows a small-amplitude prediction to beat the null. The paper also has rows with positive correlation and rms above the null (+0.12 with 0.439; Chebyshev +0.18 with 0.291), so the geometry does not "explain" both statements.
fix: Rewrite as: "is consistent with the two statements appearing together: when the cosine is zero or negative no nonzero prediction can beat the null, and when it is small and positive only a prediction of very small amplitude ($\norm{\bm p}<2\norm{\bm d}\cos\theta$) can. This is a guide, since the paper's corr is the centered (Pearson) cosine."

quote: Now recall the geometry of the triple product from first-year physics \cite{hrw}
problem: The bible's reader knows only components, dot product and magnitude of 3D vectors. The cross product is not in the assumed list (the chapter adds it to its own prerequisites), and the scalar triple product is not first-year material. The component formula for r2×r3 and the fact that |r2×r3| is the parallelogram area are used without derivation.
fix: Either define the cross product by components here and show in two lines that it is perpendicular to both factors with magnitude |a||b| sin θ, or drop the triple-product route and put the volume interpretation in the `beyond` box with the other determinant properties.

quote: is the volume of the parallelepiped spanned by the rows.
problem: The 2D discussion and the key idea ("volume scaling factor of A", "columns are dependent") are about columns, but the 3D argument gives the volume spanned by the rows. The link is det A^T = det A (property D7), which comes later and is not invoked.
fix: Add: "By property (D7) below, $\det A^\top=\det A$, so this is also the volume spanned by the columns, the images of the unit cube's edges; hence $\abs{\det A}$ is the volume scaling factor."

quote: So a constant correction $c_0$ shifts every level by the same $c_0$, to first order.
problem: The next sentence calls this uniform shift "the ``joint shift'' direction" in quotation marks. The paper uses "arbitrary joint shifts" (Sec. VI) for arbitrary patterns of shifts across all levels at once, not for a uniform shift. The chapter then quotes the paper's phrase in the Paper connection, so the two uses collide.
fix: Rename it "the uniform-shift direction" and remove the quotation marks. In the Paper connection, gloss the paper's phrase as "arbitrary patterns of simultaneous level shifts".

quote: Table~III notes that the odd/even splits have 200 training levels at scale 1
problem: The quoted words "so the rows with M≥200 are saturated" come from the Sec. III paragraph "Within-height splits", not from Table III (whose caption is worded differently). The chapter also omits that the saturated M=200 rows have in-sample rms 0.176/0.171, far from zero, which matters for the full-rank argument.
fix: Change to "Sec.~III (Within-height splits) notes ..." and add: "the square case $M=200$ still leaves in-sample rms 0.176 and 0.171, so saturation by count does not by itself give an exact fit."

quote: in which shuffled and phase-randomized targets are fitted as well as the true zeros
problem: Three in-sample numbers follow but only two surrogate types are named. The third (0.138 ± 0.005) is the amplitude-adjusted (IAAFT) surrogate.
fix: Write "in which permuted, phase-randomized and amplitude-adjusted surrogate targets are fitted as well as the true zeros (in-sample rms ..., respectively)".

quote: and $A(B+C)=AB+AC$ (from \cref{eq:linear-algebra-matmul}, since each entry is a sum)
problem: Matrix addition and multiplication of a matrix by a scalar are never defined, yet they are used here and in $(ad-bc)\,I$ and the $1/(ad-bc)$ prefactor of the 2×2 inverse.
fix: Add when matrices are introduced: "Matrices of the same shape are added entry by entry, $(A+B)_{ij}=A_{ij}+B_{ij}$, and scaled entry by entry, $(sA)_{ij}=sA_{ij}$." Then show the one-line index proof of distributivity.

problem: The sum-of-squares formula is used without proof or reference. The bible forbids unstated results, and this chapter may assume only Chapter 2.
fix: Add a short justification, for example the telescoping sum of $(j+1)^3-j^3=3j^2+3j+1$, or state it as a standard calculus result and verify it for n=3 and n=4.

quote: If $\bar p=\frac1n\sum_jp_j$ and $\bm 1=(1,\dots,1)$, then
problem: The symbol $\bar d$ appears in the correlation formula but is never defined. The case where a centered vector is zero (a constant prediction such as the null) is also not mentioned; corr is undefined there.
fix: Write "If $\bar p=\frac1n\sum_jp_j$ and $\bar d=\frac1n\sum_jd_j$ are the component means ..." and add "(defined when neither centered vector is zero)".

quote: choose the length $\alpha$ of $\bm p=\alpha\hat{\bm p}$ to minimize the error
problem: α is called a length, but the minimizer α = ‖d‖ cos θ is negative when cos θ < 0 (the direction flips).
fix: Say "choose the signed amplitude $\alpha$ (negative $\alpha$ reverses the direction)".

quote: the eigenvectors of a non-Hermitian matrix are complex
problem: "Eigenvectors" and "non-Hermitian" are used before either is defined. Eigenvectors are previewed and Hermitian is defined only three sections later.
fix: Rephrase: "and in the paper's Sec.~II~E certain special vectors of a complex matrix (eigenvectors, defined in Chapter~\ref{ch:eigen}) have complex components".

quote: Choose $c_0=s$ as the free variable.
problem: By the chapter's own definition, free variables are the non-pivot columns after elimination, which here is c_3 (pivots fall in columns 0, 1, 2). Choosing c_0 without comment contradicts the procedure just taught.
fix: Add: "(Elimination would make $c_3$ the free variable; any one of the four can be used to parametrize the line of solutions, and $c_0$ is the most convenient here.)"

quote: the same equations give the closest function in the span
problem: The claim that the Gram equations give the best approximation when f is outside the span is asserted without derivation, yet Answer 17 relies on it.
fix: Add one line: "requiring the residual $f-\sum_ka_k\phi_k$ to be orthogonal to every $\phi_j$, the closest-point condition of \cref{eq:linear-algebra-closest}, gives exactly these equations". Or mark it explicitly as proved in Chapter~\ref{ch:least-squares}.

quote: The determinant is the factor by which $A$ scales areas
problem: This is shown only for the unit square. The extension to arbitrary regions is asserted.
fix: Add: "By linearity every small grid square is mapped to a copy of this parallelogram, so any region built from such squares has its area multiplied by the same factor."

quote: in which case $A$ is the zero matrix, which has no inverse
problem: The statement is given without a reason.
fix: Append: "since $0\cdot X=0\ne I$ for every $X$".

quote: Every numerical calculation later in this book ultimately reduces to operations on matrices.
problem: This is false as stated: root finding for the smooth zeros and evaluating the prime sum are not matrix operations.
fix: Delete the sentence (along with the box), or soften to "Many of the numerical calculations later in this book ...".

quote: the one used with the bra--ket notation
problem: The bible allows en dashes only for numeric ranges and paired names. "bra--ket" and "matrix--vector product" (subsection title) are neither.
fix: Use hyphens: "bra-ket", "matrix-vector product".

quote: "How far is my prediction from the truth?" becomes the length of a difference vector.
problem: Straight double quotes in LaTeX typeset as two closing quotes. This occurs three times in the chapter introduction.
fix: Use ``...'' for all three quoted questions.

quote: the first column is again $1$, but the rest of the matrix is no longer sparse
problem: This is a numerical claim about the Wu--Sprung sensitivity matrix from the chapter's own computation, but the CHECKS script has no assertion for it.
fix: Add a check that builds A for the Wu--Sprung potential with `qmnt.wu_sprung_V`, `qmnt.grid` and `qmnt.fd_levels(..., return_vectors=True)`, then asserts column 0 equals 1 and that many off-diagonal entries exceed a threshold.

quote: first column 1, A[n-1, n] = +-0.5
problem: With nlev = M = 6 the entry A[5, 6] does not exist; level 6 has only the 1 in column 0. The comment invites an index error.
fix: Change the comment to "# first column 1; A[n-1, n] = +-0.5 for n <= M-1".

quote: elimination (LU) inside LAPACK
problem: "LU" and "LAPACK" are not defined in this chapter or in any assumed one.
fix: Change the comment to "# Gaussian elimination, done by a standard library routine", or add one sentence defining LAPACK as the standard linear-algebra library behind numpy.
